title: How I got highlighted by OpenAI in their pretraining competition
description: CaseOps, phased test-time training, and making the most of 16 MB.
markdown:
OpenAI [highlighted my CaseOps tokenizer](https://openai.com/index/what-parameter-golf-taught-us/) in its Parameter Golf write-up, in the section on new modeling and data ideas. The idea was small: stop making a tiny language model learn separate vocabulary for the same word in different cases.

The other contribution I want to talk about is phased test-time training. It lets the model carry something useful from one evaluation document into the next.

These were the two most interesting things I contributed to the competition. One changes how text is represented. The other changes when the model gets to learn.

## A language model in 16 MB

[Parameter Golf](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf) asked us to train the best language model we could fit into a 16 MB artifact, including the counted code and compressed weights. Training had to finish within ten minutes on eight H100s. Evaluation got its own ten-minute budget.

The score was bits per byte on held-out FineWeb text. Lower is better: how many bits does the model need, on average, to encode a byte of the original text?

That makes tokenization unusually interesting. You can change the vocabulary or the representation, but you still pay for predicting the same original text. Under a small memory budget, the question becomes how much of the model's capacity is going toward useful distinctions.

## CaseOps

Consider these:

```text
apple
Apple
APPLE
```

They share almost all their structure. A conventional case-sensitive vocabulary can spend separate entries on those variants, or break them into different subword sequences. Either way, capitalization gets tangled up with the lexical representation.

CaseOps separates the two. The lexical stream is lowercase; a small set of operators preserves the casing.

```text
apple  → apple
Apple  → [TITLE]apple
APPLE  → [ALLCAPS]apple
```

Now the tokenizer can reuse the same lowercase pieces, while the model learns a reusable capitalization operation.

This is a reversible transform before SentencePiece BPE. The representation still contains every capital letter. The model has to predict the operators too.

### Four small operators

The [implementation](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/blob/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-18_PR1626_CaseOps_Taper/lossless_caps.py) works over runs of ASCII letters:

- **TITLE** capitalizes the first letter of a run.
- **ALLCAPS** capitalizes the whole run.
- **CAPNEXT** capitalizes the next letter, for mixed-case words.
- **ESC** escapes a literal control character.

Lowercase runs pass through unchanged. Non-ASCII characters also pass through unchanged. The operators are reserved characters in the actual transform; the names below make them readable.

<!--CASEOPS_DEMO-->

Mixed case makes the benefit a little less tidy. A name like OpenAI needs multiple operations. But title case and all-caps words have short descriptions, and the transform gives us those descriptions directly.

The useful bias is that spelling and casing can share structure. Learning what “apple” means no longer has to be completely separate from learning how to capitalize it. With only 8,192 vocabulary entries, that is an appealing place to save duplication.

### Counting the original bytes

There is one important bookkeeping detail. The transformed stream has a different byte length, so scoring against its bytes would change the task.

The exporter writes a byte-count sidecar alongside the validation tokens. The evaluator uses those counts to charge the prediction loss against the **original UTF-8 bytes**. Capitalization operators still cost prediction bits; inserting them doesn't inflate the denominator.

```math
\mathrm{BPB}=\frac{\text{total negative log-likelihood in nats}}
{\ln(2)\times\text{original byte count}}.
```

The [exporter and record README](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/tree/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-18_PR1626_CaseOps_Taper) have the transform, reserved-symbol configuration, and byte-accounting details.

My [CaseOps submission](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1729) finished at **1.06780 BPB** averaged over three seeds, in about **15.94 MB**. It combined the tokenizer with a mild late weight-decay taper on the existing phased-TTT stack. That number belongs to the whole submission.

What I like about CaseOps is how little machinery it needs. The transformer stays a transformer. We just give it a representation with less duplicated structure to learn.

## Phased test-time training

The competition allowed a useful form of online learning: once a token had been scored, the model could train on it to help predict future tokens. Its original score stayed fixed.

Earlier work by [samacqua](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1530) already used this inside each document. Score a chunk, update a LoRA adapter using that chunk, then predict the next one. At the document boundary, reset the adapter.

That gives the model a short-lived memory of the current document. My addition was to let the shared base model learn across documents as well.

### Two timescales

Document-local adaptation is good at picking up the topic, terminology, and style of the text you're currently reading. But resetting the adapter throws that adaptation away.

The base model offers a second place to put learning. It can absorb changes from already-scored documents and pass them on to later ones. Local LoRA still handles the specifics of each new document.

My [first phased implementation](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1610) kept the existing evaluator and inserted one pause:

1. Score documents using the usual per-document LoRA adaptation.
2. After 2,000 documents have completed in the evaluation queue, gather those documents.
3. Run distributed SGD on that already-scored prefix to update the base model.
4. Resume the queue with the updated base and fresh local adapters for subsequent documents.

<!--TTT_DIAGRAM-->

The ordering is the whole trick. The global update only sees documents whose scores are already counted. It improves the starting point for later predictions without going back and changing earlier scores.

### Why phases

I initially tried a more continuous combination of local and global updates. It was harder to make that run efficiently across GPUs: synchronizing the shared base model kept getting in the way of the local work.

A phase boundary makes that coordination much simpler. The GPUs finish a defined amount of scoring, do a shared training job, then return to scoring. It also makes the information flow easy to follow: everything entering global SGD has already been evaluated.

The [original record](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/blob/main/records/track_10min_16mb/2026-04-13_VarLenAttn_PhasingTTT2000/README.md) left training unchanged and moved the three-seed mean from **1.07336388 to 1.07280628 BPB**, with evaluation taking about 507 seconds on average. A small improvement, with an extra learning mechanism that others could build on.

And they did. [dexhunter's next version](https://github.com/openai/parameter-golf/pull/1626) extended the idea to three phases, alternating scoring and global SGD several times. That was the stack I later built the CaseOps submission on.

I like that loop: contribute an idea, someone improves it, then their improvement becomes the starting point for your next experiment.

## Sharing what can be shared

CaseOps and phased TTT solve different problems, but both make better use of shared structure.

CaseOps shares lexical pieces across capitalization patterns. Phased TTT shares learning across documents while preserving a separate, fast adaptation path for each one.

The constraints made both ideas worth trying. With a much larger model or a much longer run, it is easy to leave a bit of duplication or unused learning on the table. Sixteen megabytes and a ten-minute clock make you notice it.

And sometimes a few capitalization operators are enough to get your tokenizer into OpenAI's write-up.

title: Reverse engineering DiMuon through a training API
description: Turning a language-model API into a matrix test bench, finding the update rule, and getting sidetracked by floating point.
markdown:
A language-model API is a strange place to reverse engineer a matrix optimizer. You can't hand it a matrix. You hand it tokens and a loss, then look at how the weights moved. Thinking Machines added DiMuon to Tinker with [a learning rate, momentum and gradient clipping](https://tinker-docs.thinkingmachines.ai/tinker/optimizers/), but no update equations. I wanted to see how much of it we could work out from the outside. The answer turned out to have a nice shape: **scale the momentum's rows and columns, apply a polar transform, apply the same scaling again, then set the update's length.** Finding that rule was one project. Getting the numbers to agree was another. The second one ended with an exact dot product and a disagreement with a GPU. Part 1 / The optimizer ## A small, trainable detour LoRA keeps the original model weight fixed and learns a change through two smaller matrices, A and B. A squeezes the input into a few coordinates; B expands it back out. The number of coordinates is the adapter's **rank**. The effective weight is W₀ + sBA, where s is a scale factor. That skinny detour is all the optimizer gets to change. [Muon](https://kellerjordan.github.io/posts/muon/) takes a momentum matrix and approximately makes its nonzero singular values equal. Instead of letting one large direction dominate, it spreads the update across the available directions. A short matrix-polynomial iteration approximates this **polar transform**. Applying ordinary Muon to A and B was our starting guess. But the version we tried gave the tall B factor a much larger step than A. DiMuon gave both factors the same update norm. Even after rescaling our Muon predictions, the directions were still off by about 20% at the median. There was more going on than a different learning rate. ## Making the API answer small questions First, we needed a gradient meter. The idea came from [Martin Marek's StableReinforce thread](https://x.com/mrtnm/status/2114145574987702525): use a carefully chosen Adam step to read gradients from downloaded weights. With both Adam betas set to zero, a large epsilon makes the update almost linear in the gradient. The exact equation is invertible. Adam becomes a measuring instrument.
The gradient-meter equations With no clipping or weight decay, a coordinate moves by: ```math u=-\eta\frac{g}{|g|+\epsilon}, \qquad g=-\frac{\epsilon u}{\eta-|u|}. ``` Large epsilon avoids saturation. We repeated measurements with different epsilon values to check the recovered gradients, including their rounding.
Then LoRA gave us a convenient way to simplify the model. At initialization, B is zero. The gradient of A is therefore zero too. If the adapter is on the output projection, the transformer supplies a fixed feature h, and the trainable part is just **sBAh**. From B's point of view, the language model is a linear system. We used signed token weights that sum to zero. This cancels cross-entropy's shared log-sum-exp term, leaving a linear combination of logits. Combining calibrated contexts gave us useful matrix patterns inside that linear system. The best experiments made most of the optimizer irrelevant: - **Change history without changing weights.** Take steps with learning rate zero. Then set beta to zero on the measured step. Ordinary momentum forgets the history—but DiMuon still responds to it. - **Cancel signed history.** Make old gradients oppose each other. The scaling follows the old signed momentum, rather than an average of squared gradients. - **Make the polar response cancel.** Give it two equal axes, then compare their ratio after the update. That last one is my favorite. We didn't need an exact polar implementation to identify the scaling after it. Symmetry had removed that unknown from the experiment. ## The sandwich Here's the rule we arrived at. The current gradient feeds an ordinary momentum EMA. The **previous momentum** supplies row and column statistics. Those statistics scale the matrix both before and after the polar transform. The final operation sets the update norm, so the taller LoRA factor doesn't automatically get a much bigger step. Why use the old momentum? It gives the optimizer a slowly changing picture of which coordinates have been active, using state it already keeps. There is no separate second-moment EMA or extra beta in this construction. Rows and columns with more old momentum get smaller multipliers. The polar transform chooses a direction in those rescaled coordinates; applying the multipliers again maps that direction back. The last normalization chooses its length. This is also a useful geometric interpretation: an ideal polar factor is a steepest-descent direction under an operator-norm constraint. The diagonal sandwich changes the geometry of that constraint. On LoRA's skinny matrices, collecting these row and column statistics is cheap.
The complete update equations After optional joint gradient clipping, form the current momentum: ```math M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\widetilde G_t. ``` Compute energies from the previous momentum: ```math e_i=\sum_j M_{t-1,ij}^2, \qquad f_j=\sum_i M_{t-1,ij}^2. ``` Normalize each vector by its maximum, add a small ridge, and take the inverse fourth root: ```math D_r=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{e_i}{\max_k e_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right], ``` ```math D_c=\operatorname{diag}\left[\left(\frac{f_j}{\max_k f_k}+10^{-4}\right)^{-1/4}\right]. ``` Zero old momentum uses relative energies of one. The ridge keeps inactive coordinates from getting unbounded multipliers. Energy is a squared norm, so its inverse fourth root is an inverse square root of the norm. Then: ```math U_t=D_r\,\Phi(D_rM_tD_c)\,D_c, \qquad \Delta\theta_t=-\eta C(r)\frac{U_t}{\|U_t\|_F}. ``` Φ includes the approximate polar computation and its input normalization. A zero direction gets a zero update. At alpha 32, tested ranks 1 through 64 followed: ```math C(r)=\sqrt r\left(\frac r{32}\right)^{0.175}. ``` This predicted a held-out rank-16 norm to about 5.6 × 10⁻⁸ relative error. The origin of 0.175 is still a mystery.
A LoRA wrinkle is that multiplying A by c and dividing B by c leaves BA unchanged. The optimizer still sees different factor coordinates. Equal-sized A and B updates don't automatically mean equal-sized changes to the effective model weight. Part 2 / The numerics detour ## Same equation, different answer Once the rule looked right, we wanted the numbers to line up. Close was less interesting than figuring out exactly why they differed. Almost-canceling gradients exposed the momentum storage: the current calculation needed FP32, while the state carried into the next step behaved as BF16. Tiny coordinates exposed intermediate FP16 stores in the polar iteration. Those coordinates barely affected the total error, but their ratios made the rounding choice obvious. Our spectral replay used five stages from the published [Polar Express v3 coefficients](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.16932v3), evaluated in Horner form. Algebraically equivalent expressions gave different answers once intermediate rounding entered the picture.
The polar computation we replayed Normalize the preconditioned momentum and store it in FP16: ```math X=\operatorname{round}_{\mathrm{FP16}}\left( \frac{D_rM_tD_c}{1.01\max(\|D_rM_tD_c\|_F,10^{-7})} \right). ``` For a tall matrix, form the small Gram matrix R = XᵀX and apply a stage: ```math X\leftarrow X\left[aI+R(bI+cR)\right]. ``` The coefficients change each stage. Wide matrices use the transposed construction. The intermediate stores matter, as does how the GPU reduces each matrix product.
One SST2 update still had a 0.79% spectral direction error on CPU. Moving the same equations to an H100 brought that case to about **7.7 × 10⁻⁸**. All 2,913 previously mismatched inferred FP16 output values matched. The first Gram matrix had changed by one rounding step. The polynomial amplified it. That case didn't need another optimizer term; it needed the right arithmetic. Even two GPU paths could disagree. Their matrix multiplications split dot products into different groups before adding the partial results. Reproducing those partitions and their FP16 partial-result storage reproduced both paths in our B-factor controls. ## Checking the measuring instrument The API itself added another puzzle. Identical exported weights and matching selected log-probabilities didn't always give identical measured gradients. In one group of four measurements, three agreed and the fourth differed across all 253 B factors. Small probes exposed a difference in accumulation: round each contribution before adding, or add the FP32 products and round once afterward. The latter reproduced **12,068,664 eligible values with zero mismatches** in one measured regime. At B = 0, a single-example B gradient also gives us a peek inside the model. It is a rounded outer product between a backward signal and the projected activation Ah. Every rounded value supplies an interval constraint on that projection. Change A's seed while keeping B zero, and you get a second instrument looking at the same effective model. This caught a hidden vector that passed the first probe and failed the second. Eight coordinates had missed a difference in a 4,096-dimensional vector. Then one dot product landed almost exactly on a BF16 rounding boundary. Its inputs were binary floats, so we could calculate it exactly with integer arithmetic. We had been looking for a model difference when part of the problem was how we were measuring it. The next step was to carry the local model forward through more layers, checking both instruments along the way. Even `rsqrt(x)` versus `1 / sqrt(x)` mattered. Using the latter in FP32 normalization reproduced our double-precision reference through 19 full first-token blocks, before another probe disagreed inside block 20. One rounding decision had been hiding behind passing projections, then propagating into later layers. ## Following real gradients through four updates The cleanest optimizer demonstration uses four SST2 steps with rank-one LoRA on Qwen3-8B's output projection. The local optimizer carries its own momentum and weights, while consuming gradients measured at the hosted states. We reran the unchanged reconstruction on a fresh H100. Every recovered FP16 spectral value matched again. After four steps, the largest absolute difference in the accumulated weights was **9.3 × 10⁻¹⁰**.
How we measured such small errors The ordinary steps use learning rate 0.001. Subtracting two nearly equal exported weights loses precision, so we also measure updates with the learning rate enlarged to 16. That changes the readout gain while keeping the optimizer state and gradient fixed. The diagnostic update errors above come from those high-gain measurements. At the ordinary learning rate, errors in the subtracted updates range from roughly 2 × 10⁻⁶ to 2.4 × 10⁻⁵; the accumulated local weights differ from the hosted weights by at most 9.3 × 10⁻¹⁰. Repeated executions and independently measured gradients check the comparison.
That is an optimizer replay. The stronger experiment is two ordinary training runs, each computing its own gradients at its own evolving weights. Matching the model's forward and backward arithmetic is still in the way of that one. There are optimizer cases left to explain too: a rank-two B continuation differs by **0.81%**, and the historical A cases by **1.14% RMS**. The four-step result doesn't make those disappear. The fun part was learning how to ask better questions. A cold LoRA factor gave us a linear system. Zero learning rate separated history from weights. Symmetry canceled an unknown transform. Tiny coordinates exposed rounding. A second projection caught what the first missed. We started with a LoRA optimizer and ended up calculating an exact dot product to settle an argument with a GPU. A good detour.
